newsitem.title: LATVIA: Latvia's Air Baltic says first year below target.
newsitem.headline: Latvia's Air Baltic says first year below target.

text.p: Latvian airline Air Baltic, which is nearly a third-owned by Scandinavian Airlines, on Tuesday marked its first year of operation but said it has slightly undershot its own expectations.
The company was formed from Latvia's old state airline and the government owns 51 percent, SAS has 29 percent and Swedfund and the Danish Investment Fund also own stakes.
Air Baltic president and chief executive officer Kjell Fredheim said the company had been aiming at a load factor of 50 percent by the summer but had only gained 44 to 45 percent.

"In one area I admit I made a miscalculation and that was to do with the stamp of being an eastern European airline," Fredheim told Reuters after a news conference called to mark the one year anniversary of the airline.

The Baltic market has attracted increasing interest from Scandinavian and German airlines. Danish carrier Maersk recently bought Estonian Air and Finnair signed a cooperation deal with Lithuania's state-owned airline.
Fredheim said that for many passengers being 'eastern European' meant bad service, bad airplanes and bad maintenance.
Fredheim said lower than expected passenger numbers through Riga airport plus the company's failure to win rights to fly to Moscow, a key market for the Baltics, had also hit Air Baltic.
Passengers were instead choosing to fly with international airlines such as SAS, Finnair and Lufthansa.
Fredheim strongly rejected the poor image and said Air Baltic's service standards were high and that the aircraft were maintained to Western standards.
"We have managed to create an airline that is a safe and reliable operation...in the operational field I have believe we have come further than expected," Fredheim said.
The company currently flies three Avro jets and one SAAB turboprop. It has 190 employees.

Due to the lower than expected passenger loads and the onset of winter, the timetable is to be changed with fewer departures and one Avro will become free. It will be leased to an Irish airline but Fredheim did not want to name the airline.
Fredheim said that Air Baltic was fortunate in having a higher than average number of business class passengers, which he put at 40 percent, compared to a more usual 20 percent.
But he said the airline must persuade more ordinary Latvians to fly and would introduce special packages to London, the favourite destination for Latvians as they do not need visas.
He said the Helsinki, Copenhagen and Stockholm routes were the most profitable for the airline.
Under the business plan drawn up when the company was formed, Air Baltic expects to make a loss this year, break even in 1997 and become profitable in 1998.
